title: Implement strategies for behaviour change and innovation

lessons.title: How farmers adopt new practices
lessons.html:
Adoption is a process, not an event

Extension aims to help farmers change practice: plant certified seed instead of retained seed, vaccinate cattle on schedule, use conservation tillage, keep records. Changing behaviour takes time. Farmers usually move through stages before they adopt an innovation fully.

  1. Awareness: the farmer hears about the practice, for example at a farmers' day or on community radio.
  2. Interest: the farmer seeks more information and asks neighbours.
  3. Evaluation: the farmer weighs costs, risks and benefits for their own situation.
  4. Trial: the farmer tries it on a small scale, such as one camp or a quarter hectare.
  5. Adoption: the farmer uses it as standard practice, or rejects it.

Different types of adopters

In any community some farmers adopt early and others late. Innovators and early adopters are often better resourced, more connected and willing to take risks. The majority wait to see results from people they trust. Late adopters are often the most risk-averse, sometimes because one bad season could cost the family its food supply. Late adoption is often a rational choice, not ignorance.

What makes an innovation easier to adopt

  • Relative advantage: it is clearly better than the current practice, in rands or labour saved.
  • Compatibility: it fits the farmer's values, resources and farming system.
  • Simplicity: it is easy to understand and apply.
  • Trialability: it can be tested on a small scale first.
  • Observability: results are visible to neighbours.

Use these five qualities to assess any innovation before you promote it. If an innovation scores poorly on several of them, adapt it or choose a different entry point.

lessons.title: Strategies that change behaviour
lessons.html:
Choosing the right strategy

There is no single method that works for every group. Combine strategies based on the stage of adoption and the type of farmer.

For awareness and interest

  • Mass media such as community radio, WhatsApp groups and posters at the dip tank or cooperative.
  • Farmers' days and information days with short, practical talks.
  • Messages from trusted local voices, such as a respected lead farmer or traditional leader.

For evaluation and trial

  • Demonstration plots or camps managed by local farmers, comparing old and new practice side by side.
  • Farmer field schools, where a group meets regularly through a whole season to observe, test and discuss.
  • Exchange visits to farmers who already use the practice successfully.
  • Simple cost and benefit calculations in rands, using the farmer's own figures.

For adoption and maintenance

  • Follow-up visits to solve problems during the first seasons.
  • Links to inputs, credit and markets so the new practice is affordable and profitable.
  • Recognition, such as certificates or competitions for best managed herds or fields.
  • Study groups where farmers keep supporting each other.

Removing barriers

Often farmers want to change but cannot. Common barriers are lack of cash at planting time, no transport to collect inputs, unclear land tenure, labour shortages and distant markets. Identify the barrier before you push the message harder. For example, if farmers are not vaccinating, the problem may be cold chain and access to vaccine, not lack of knowledge. Solving a supply barrier through a group order may achieve more than ten more lectures.

Behaviour change is also social. When a group agrees together to a new practice, members encourage each other. Group commitment, written down and reviewed at meetings, is a powerful tool.

lessons.title: Implementing and tracking a change strategy
lessons.html:
Putting the strategy into action

A behaviour change strategy needs a clear plan. Use this simple framework:

  1. Define the target behaviour exactly, for example: members dip cattle every two weeks during summer according to the local tick control programme.
  2. Know the audience: how many farmers, what resources, what current practice and what barriers.
  3. Choose activities for each adoption stage, with dates and responsible people.
  4. Arrange support: inputs, partners, transport, demonstration sites.
  5. Set indicators to measure change.

Measuring change

LevelExample indicator
ReachNumber of farmers who attended sessions
KnowledgeFarmers who can explain the practice correctly
PracticeFarmers actually using the practice, checked on visits
ResultsChange in yield, calving rate, losses or income

Attendance alone does not prove change. Visit farms to see whether practice has changed, and collect baseline information before the programme so you can compare.

Dealing with resistance

Resistance is normal. Listen to objections, as they often show a real weakness in the innovation or a barrier you have not addressed. Adapt the practice where possible. Never pressure farmers through threats or by withholding services they are entitled to; change that is forced does not last.

Sustaining innovation

Plan for the time when you are no longer present. Train lead farmers, link groups to suppliers and buyers, and encourage farmers to keep experimenting themselves. A community that tests new ideas on its own has truly adopted innovation.

Key points

  • Adoption moves through awareness, interest, evaluation, trial and adoption.
  • Innovations spread faster when they are advantageous, compatible, simple, trialable and observable.
  • Match strategies to the adoption stage and remove practical barriers.
  • Measure actual practice and results, not attendance only.
  • Treat resistance as feedback, and never force change.
